legend: Mark found an old automaton with two buttons in his attic, which he used to play with as a child. The toy is quite rusty, but it still performs its function. When the first button is pressed, a single 0%%ZSMJ0%% appears on the screen, and when the other button is pressed, either due to age or malfunction, the automaton outputs k%%ZSMJ1%% ones at once.

Mark became curious about how many different strings of lengths from ℓ%%ZSMJ2%% to r%%ZSMJ3%% can be obtained if the automaton outputs k%%ZSMJ4%% ones when the second button is pressed. However, since the automaton is old and Mark's curiosity is great, you will have to answer q%%ZSMJ5%% queries instead of the automaton.
Since the answer to any of Mark's queries can be very large, compute it modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ6%%.
input: In the first line, you are given 2%%ZSMJ7%% integers n%%ZSMJ8%% and q%%ZSMJ9%% (1≤n,q≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ10%%) — the maximum length of the string and the number of queries.
In the next q%%ZSMJ11%% lines, three integers ℓi, ri, ki%%ZSMJ12%% are given (1≤ℓi≤ri≤n,1≤k≤n%%ZSMJ13%%) — the range of lengths and the number of ones that the automaton prints.
output: For each query, output the number of strings that the automaton can print modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ14%%.
